issues.item: Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims
issues.explanation: For a 57-year-old male with a life-threatening accident, 'people who look similar to the victims' is hard to reconcile unless multiple identifiable victims were involved; this reads more like an interpersonal/assault or disaster context than a typical accident-based trigger profile.

issues.item: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: 'I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me' implies shame/visible mark/social exposure concerns that are not supported by the rest of the selected profile. With no memory, threat, or strategy items linking to visible injury or interpersonal scrutiny, this appraisal does not fit coherently with the accident-focused triggers.

issues.item: Triggers: Loss of Control: Lack of control
issues.explanation: The profile is not clinically coherent because the formulation specifies no active edges between nodes, implying the selected nodes should not form a tightly linked PTSD pattern. However, the trigger 'Lack of control' and the appraisal 'I can no longer trust my own body' are naturally connected in a life-threatening accident presentation, and the appraisal set itself forms a strong post-traumatic meaning cluster rather than isolated components.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
issues.explanation: Within the Negative Appraisals node, the items are not contradictory, but they cluster around severe global defeat/disconnection ('Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore', 'I feel dead inside') plus somatic mistrust after accident trauma ('I can no longer trust my own body'). This is clinically plausible on its own, but together with the trigger content it implies an integrated trauma formulation that conflicts with the fully disconnected edge structure.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin
issues.explanation: The profile is clinically incoherent because the cognitive formulation specifies no active edges at all, yet the selected Triggers and Negative Appraisals imply a linked trauma network. Concrete accident reminders (car sounds, crash imagery, temperature on skin) would ordinarily connect to threat, memory, or appraisals; presenting them alongside strong post-traumatic self-appraisals without any connecting nodes is inconsistent with the formulation structure.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside
issues.explanation: Within the available nodes, the Negative Appraisals are internally coherent, and the Triggers are broadly plausible for a life-threatening accident. The main problem is cross-node/formulation mismatch: specific sensory accident triggers and severe trauma-related appraisals are both present, but the formulation says these components are not linked to each other or to any other PTSD processes.

vignette:
Daniel, a 57-year-old North American interior designer who had been divorced for several years, first experienced the trauma in what should have been a routine drive home after a late client meeting. Another car came out of nowhere at an intersection and hit his vehicle hard enough that, in his memory, everything seemed to fracture at once: the violent impact, the twisting metal, the awful sense of being trapped inside a body and a car that would not respond the way it should. In the aftermath, what stayed with him was not only the physical shock of the accident but the image of cars colliding and crumpling, a scene that later returned to him with unwanted force whenever he saw damaged vehicles on the road or in news footage. Even months later, he could feel his stomach tighten when he passed a fresh crash on the highway and caught sight of two cars pulled to the shoulder, their position enough to call the whole event back with startling immediacy.

Before the accident, Daniel had built his life around precision, aesthetics, and a strong sense of control. He moved through work with confidence, meeting clients, sketching plans, and arranging spaces with the assumption that his body and mind would cooperate with him. Afterward, he began to see himself differently. He found himself listening for car sounds in a way that felt involuntary, tense whenever engines revved too close, when tires squealed at an intersection, or when traffic noise rose abruptly outside his office windows. Those ordinary sounds no longer felt neutral to him; they carried the possibility of impact. He was especially unsettled by discussions about accidents. If a colleague mentioned a fender bender, or if a client casually told a story about a highway pileup, Daniel would grow quiet and drift away from the conversation, feeling as though his attention had been pulled back into the scene he could not shake. He did not merely dislike these moments; he experienced them as dangerous intrusions, as if hearing about another crash could drop him right back into the one that had changed his life.

As the weeks passed, Daniel became increasingly preoccupied with the sense that his own body could not be trusted. He noticed every ache, every hesitation in movement, every flutter or stiffness, and interpreted them with growing dread. A sudden twinge in his chest or a moment of lightheadedness would leave him wondering whether something inside him had been permanently altered by the accident. He had come to believe that he could no longer trust his body to remain steady or predictable, and that belief made even ordinary activities feel less secure than they once had. At times he would stand still in his own kitchen or in the middle of a project site and feel detached from the confident, capable man he remembered being. He told himself that he did not know himself anymore, that something essential had shifted in him since the crash, leaving him unfamiliar to himself in ways he struggled to put into words. More than anything, he feared that the accident had changed him for the worse in a permanent way, and that there would be no return to the person he had been before.

Those convictions shaped the way he moved through daily life. As an interior designer, Daniel still needed to visit offices, showrooms, and clients’ homes, but he did so with more strain than he let on. A site visit that required driving across town could leave him visibly tense before he even left the parking lot, especially if traffic was heavy or an ambulance sound cut through the street. He learned to scan roads for signs of collisions and to feel relieved only when he had passed safely through an intersection. He also found himself withdrawing from conversations where accidents might be mentioned, including during work lunches or informal gatherings that used to be easy for him. Over time, these habits narrowed his life. He became more guarded, less spontaneous, and more likely to decline invitations that involved long drives or unpredictable routes. Friends and former colleagues noticed he seemed changed, though Daniel experienced it more privately as a loss of continuity with his former self.

By the time he sought help, Daniel described feeling worn down by how often reminders of the crash entered his day. The sight of damaged cars, the sound of traffic, and even a casual conversation about an accident could bring on a surge of dread and a painful sense that he was no longer the person he had once been. He came to treatment not because the memories had faded, but because they had not. He was hoping for relief from the constant shock of being pulled back into that intersection, and he was most afraid that he would remain trapped in the belief that his body was unreliable and that the worst version of himself had become permanent.
